extracted.intended_audience: prospective Summer of Math Exposition (SoME1) applicants; online math/video exposition creators and educators
extracted.subtask_description: Judging and submission criteria for short-form online math exposition (video/visual lessons) submitted to the Summer of Math Exposition (SoME1) contest. Emphasizes what makes good online math exposition and who is eligible to enter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Jargon should be explained, the goals of the lesson should be understandable with minimal background."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize empathy for newcomers: make the lesson's aims and necessary background clear so viewers with minimal prior knowledge can follow. Avoid unexplained technical language; prioritize lucid explanations and accessible pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Viewers should understand why they care within the first 30 seconds."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an early hook that communicates relevance or interest quickly. The first half-minute should convey why the topic matters or why the viewer should keep watching (practical relevance, surprising fact, striking question, or intuitive tension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer an experience unavailable elsewhere — "fresh angles on familiar topics or surfacing under-explored ideas."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize original approaches, perspectives, or topic choices. Novelty can be a new pedagogy, an uncommon example, an unusual connection to other fields, or covering a topic that is rarely presented in this medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorable
rubrics_metrics.description: Content should "remain vivid months later through presentation quality, presenter enthusiasm, or striking insights."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for lasting impact via strong presentation (visuals/animation/structure), energetic or sincere delivery, and memorable takeaways or insights. Memorability is valued even if the piece is not 'rigorously formal' like a paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Created during the contest period (eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Entry must be created during the contest period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions produced outside the specified contest timeframe are ineligible. This filters for new work created specifically for the competition window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: Mathematics broadly defined
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topics touching mathematics, theoretical CS, or physics-related mathematical exposition are acceptable; the contest is not limited to narrow subfields.

rubrics_metrics.name: One submission per person/group
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants may only submit a single entry (individuals or groups). Multiple entries by the same entrant(s) are not permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language requirement: English
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions must be in English (or otherwise meet the contest's stated language requirement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility: Publicly available and free
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitted works must be available to the public without paywalls (e.g., free on public platforms) so judges and the public can view them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection process / judging procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review phase, pre-filtering for a manageable judging pool, final judges evaluate using the four criteria; judges allocate ~5–10 minutes per entry for longer works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial peer review: entrants rate ~5 submissions each to surface promising entries. Organizers pre-filter to reduce the pool before final judging. Final judges use the four-axis rubric (clarity, motivation, novelty, memorability) when evaluating and may spend only a few minutes per entry in the final pass—plan submissions to make strong impressions quickly.
